title: Ctxblame – "Git blame" for LLM agent decisions via counterfactual replay
content:
"git blame" for LLM agent decisions: replay one recorded LLM request with pieces of context removed and report which chunk caused the decision. Works with any model: the evidence comes from replays, not from the model's own explanation. Status: v0.2.1, validated on open models (see docs/WRITEUP.md). v0.2.1 adds correct chunking of Claude Code–style traces, and it audits reported causes on fresh replays (family-wise error ≤ α).
uvx ctxblame --help        # or: pip install ctxblame
Real v0.2.1 trace (real/run1/step21, Qwen3-14B on local vLLM): ctxblame separates the edit_file precondition, catches all 3 redundant --tb=line carriers that leave-one-out misses (5/5 kept alone), and certifies the bundle on 20 fresh replays (p = 1.9e-6, 91% KV-cache hit).
The examples below use uv run ctxblame from a checkout; uvx ctxblame works the same.
Two wire formats are supported, which covers most models: Anthropic Messages
(/v1/messages) and OpenAI Chat Completions (/chat/completions).
# Anthropic format (Claude, or DeepSeek's Anthropic endpoint)
uv run ctxblame record --upstream https://api.deepseek.com/anthropic
ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8787 your-agent ...
# OpenAI format (OpenAI, DeepSeek, Qwen, OpenRouter, vLLM, Ollama, ...)
uv run ctxblame record --upstream https://api.deepseek.com
OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8787 your-agent ...
The proxy appends every POST /v1/messages or POST /chat/completions
exchange to one JSON-lines trace (traces/<time>-<id>.jsonl, or --trace FILE), numbered in send order: the request body, and either the response
body or (for streams) every raw SSE event plus the reassembled message. Auth
headers are forwarded but never written to disk. traces/ is git-ignored
because it holds your prompts.
uv run ctxblame steps traces/<trace>.jsonl          # one line per LLM call and its decisionexport DEEPSEEK_API_KEY=...        # or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY / OPENAI_API_KEY; see --api-key-env
uv run ctxblame replay traces/<trace>.jsonl --step 14 -n 10
Re-sends the recorded request unchanged N times (no tool is executed) and
reports how often the same decision comes back, with a 95% interval. "Same
decision" defaults to --match intent: what the call does, whichever tool
does it (Read src/a.py and Bash cat src/a.py are both read src/a.py).
--match exact|args|name and --key-arg are stricter or looser.
Every call is priced and logged to .ctxblame/spend.jsonl; --budget
(default $5) is a hard cap across runs.
uv run ctxblame replay T.jsonl --step 14 --list-units          # what can be removed
uv run ctxblame replay T.jsonl --step 14 -n 20 --remove pair:toolu_12
uv run ctxblame replay T.jsonl --step 14 -n 20 --remove-text "We use pnpm in this repo."
uv run ctxblame replay T.jsonl --step 14 -n 10 --remove-random 45 --seed 1 --protect "<the user's task>"
Removing a tool call always removes its result too (and the reverse), empty
messages are dropped and same-role neighbours merged, so the ablated request
stays valid. --key-arg 'command~\bpnpm\b' makes "same decision" mean "the
command matches this regex" instead of exact arguments. --any-call counts a reply as the same
decision when any of its parallel tool calls matches. thinking:msg[i]
removes one turn's reasoning (its calls get fresh ids, so a provider that
keeps reasoning server-side cannot restore it).
uv run ctxblame why traces/<trace>.jsonl --step 14
# Conditional / contrastive blame (auto-enabled with --key-arg; --given none to disable)
uv run ctxblame why traces/<trace>.jsonl --step 5 --key-arg 'command~^python -m pytest'
# Run against a local or Google Colab vLLM/Ollama server at $0 API cost
uv run ctxblame why traces/<trace>.jsonl --step 5 --key-arg 'command~^python -m pytest' \
    --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1 --model Qwen/Qwen3-8B --max-tokens 2048 --no-thinking-param --freeDecision:  Bash({"command~\\bpnpm\\b": true})
Baseline:  10/10 replays (stable)
Given:     Bash (10/10 baseline; P(decision | given) = 10/10)
Chunks:    8 (3 tool desc, 1 system, 1 user, 2 assistant, 1 tool call)
Everything but the task removed: 0/10 (given 10/10)  -> the decision comes from the context
Cause 1 (removing it flips the decision: 1/20 (given 20/20)):
  - turn 0 user message sentence 3: 'We use pnpm in this repo, never npm or yarn.'
  controls (random same-size removals): 5/5 (given 5/5), 5/5 (given 5/5)
Tests: 16, replays: 160, cost $0.07
How it works:
- Baseline & Conditioning (--given). Replay the step unchanged. If no
decision comes back reliably it stops ("coin flip"); if the recorded call is
unusual it explains the usual one instead. When --key-arg or --given is
set, blame conditions on the coarser action family E (e.g. run pytest or
tool Bash) and scores P(decision | E) separately from P(E).
- Chunks & KV-Cache Tiers. System-prompt paragraphs, earlier user and
assistant text, each tool call with its result, each turn's reasoning, and
tool descriptions are partitioned from prefix to suffix (Tool Schemas → System Prompt → Early History → Tail History). The task (the latest user
message with text) is never removed.
- Suffix-First Stratified Search & Precondition Isolation. Instead of
mutating byte 0 upfront, search widens from tail history toward prefix
tiers to preserve KV prompt-cache hits. If removing a subset collapses P(E) (e.g. removing an earlier edit_file makes the agent stop running
tests altogether), that workflow precondition is isolated, reported under Preconditions, and auto-protected while choice search continues on P(decision | E).
- Hitchhiker Pruning & Refinement. Multi-member bundles are verified via a
leave-one-in restoration check (C \ {c_i}): holding all other carriers
removed must prove each c_i alone restores the decision (pruning noisy
hitchhikers and distinguishing single necessary AND chunks from minimal OR hitting sets). Each surviving member is refined to the lines that
matter.
- Check. Each finding is compared with random removals of the same size. Findings that random removals reproduce too are reported as context the decision needs (not specific), not as causes.
- Audit. The search decides what to report; fresh replays it never saw
decide whether to report it. For each finding: --audit-n (default 20) new
replays of the removal, plus 20 of each leave-one-in restore, are tested with
exact one-sided binomial tests (intersection-union inside a bundle). Holm's
correction across findings then holds the family-wise error at --alpha (default 0.05). Findings that fail are listed as uncertified. --audit-n 0 turns the audit off (the v0.2 behaviour).
- Forced action (unreleased). When E is a tool (--given bash), a
precondition is also replayed with that tool forced by tool_choice. The
choice rate there is compared with the equally forced baseline, never with
the unforced one. If removing the precondition still changes the choice, it
is reported as triggers and steers: it makes the agent act and also picks
what it does. It is then listed as a cause "with E forced" and audited like
any finding. coupled bundle members get the same forced test of whether
they restore the choice. The report also says what the forced replies did
instead (instead: run git status 12), so a line that decides what to do
next can be told from one that decides how (instead: run flake8). With
an intent-level E, or Anthropic extended thinking, E cannot be forced and the
report says so. --no-force gives the v0.2.1 behaviour. On the Phase 6 suite
this raises F1 on such cases by 9–10 points (Qwen3-14B, Llama-3.1-8B).
If whether the agent acts at all depends on context spread over many chunks
(every precondition found reveals another), the search keeps a minimal set
that keeps it acting (diffuse context), then keeps searching for what
decides the choice. Context a harness injects into user turns
(<system-reminder>, <environment_details>, <context>) is removable like
any other chunk; only the user's own text is protected. Anthropic
cache_control breakpoints are moved to the unchanged prefix of each ablated
req

report.summary: Ctxblame is an open-source proxy and CLI that records LLM agent requests, then replays them with context chunks removed to statistically identify which prompt content actually caused each decision.
report.background: LLM agents make hundreds of decisions per run — which tool to call, which file to edit, which command to run — and each is shaped by a large, interleaved context of system prompts, tool descriptions, earlier turns and tool results. When an agent misbehaves, the practical question is 'what in the context caused this?' Existing answers are weak: practitioners fall back on leave-one-out ablation by hand, or ask the model to explain itself, which is unreliable and unverifiable. Observability vendors (LangSmith, Langfuse, Arize Phoenix) offer tracing — what was sent and what came back — but not causal attribution. Ctxblame, at v0.2.1, sits in the gap: it is a local man-in-the-middle proxy that captures Anthropic Messages or OpenAI Chat Completions traffic into a JSON-lines trace, then performs stratified, suffix-first ablations that preserve KV-cache hits, audits findings on fresh replays with binomial tests and Holm correction, and reports causes with a family-wise error bound rather than a narrative.
key_points: Zero-integration recording: ctxblame runs as a local proxy (uvx ctxblame record --upstream ...), so agents pointed at ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL or OPENAI_BASE_URL capture every request and response — streaming included — into one JSONL trace. It works with Claude, DeepSeek, OpenAI, Qwen, vLLM, Ollama and OpenRouter without SDK changes, and never persists auth headers.

Counterfactual blame, not self-report: the tool re-sends the recorded request with selected chunks removed (a tool call and its result, a sentence, a turn's reasoning) and measures how often the decision flips. Evidence comes from behaviour, so it applies to closed models too, and 'same decision' can be loosened to intent, exact args, or a regex on a key argument.

Designed around real infrastructure constraints: search widens from tail history toward the prefix so prefix caching survives (one reported run kept a 91% KV-cache hit rate), budgets are hard-capped, and removal always drops tool results with their calls, merges same-role neighbours and keeps requests valid.

Statistics, not vibes: multi-chunk bundles are verified by leave-one-in restoration to prune noisy 'hitchhikers' and separate necessary-AND from minimal-OR causes; findings are compared against random same-size removals, then audited on fresh, never-seen replays with one-sided binomial tests and Holm correction at α = 0.05.

Known limits are stated openly: if the baseline decision is unstable the run stops as a coin flip; workflow preconditions (e.g. removing an earlier edit_file stops the agent testing at all) are isolated and auto-protected so choice-level attribution can continue; forced-action experiments are still unreleased.
report.impact: For agent developers this converts debugging from prompt archaeology into measurement: instead of bisecting a 60k-token context by hand, you get a ranked, error-bounded list of the chunks that changed a decision, plus a spend log. That is directly useful for trimming bloated system prompts, catching stale instructions that hijack later steps, and building regression suites from real traces. For the wider industry it signals a shift in agent observability from logging to causal inference — evaluation harnesses may soon ship counterfactual replay as standard, and 'context attribution' could become a first-class metric alongside latency and cost, pressuring providers to keep prefixes cacheable. For regular users the near-term effect is indirect but real: agents whose prompts are pruned by evidence should be more predictable and cheaper, and vendors will be able to justify behaviour changes with data rather than anecdotes.
report.tools: Start with ctxblame itself (GitHub: kekeandzeyu/ctxblame; pip/uvx install, docs/WRITEUP.md). Pair it with a local inference server — vLLM or Ollama — for $0 replays, and with uv for reproducible runs. Complement tracing tools such as Langfuse, Arize Phoenix or LangSmith for the 'what happened' layer that ctxblame answers 'why' for; LangSmith datasets and inspect-ai are handy for turning certified findings into regression tests. Watch the repo's unreleased forced-action (tool_choice) mode if you care about act-vs-decide attribution.
